title: Project Bridgeline
goal: Take Bridgeline from a lab prototype to a trusted platform that every Halden India site can use, and win the Leadership Review’s approval before the quarter closes.
intro: At Halden Aerospace India’s Bengaluru engineering centre, engineers lose hours every week chasing test data across inboxes and spreadsheets. Your small team has a prototype that could connect engineers, test cells and suppliers in one place, and the Leadership Review is six weeks away. Your CEO decides every step, but only your four leads can see what is coming, and each of them sees only part of the picture. Share what you know, compare, and trust wisely.

d1.title: The Whiteboard Idea
d1.scene: Monday morning at the Bengaluru engineering centre. Three engineers are hunting for the same engine-test result across inboxes and spreadsheets, again. On the whiteboard, your team has sketched Bridgeline, a shared space where engineers, test cells and suppliers can post what they find. You have a small budget and plenty of enthusiasm. How do you begin?

options.label: Spend a day shadowing three engineers before writing any code
options.aftermath: The engineers show you their private trackers and the exact moment each day goes wrong. Your first screens almost write themselves.

options.label: Build a quick demo from the data you already have
options.aftermath: The demo looks good, but the data is stale and the engineers politely list what is missing.

options.label: Announce Bridgeline to the whole centre at the next all-hands
options.aftermath: The announcement earns applause and a dozen new demands. Nobody is quite sure what Bridgeline actually does.

seer: Past internal tools launched with a big announcement went quiet within a month. The ones that began with a pain people already felt kept growing.
Look back at earlier tools: loud launches faded, while those rooted in a daily frustration spread by word of mouth.
scout: The sample data is out of date, and the test-cell logs use three different formats. Two engineers already keep private trackers that work surprisingly well.
Nothing you could demo today reflects the real test logs. Meanwhile, a couple of engineers have built their own trackers that people genuinely use.
scholar: The quality archive notes that tools designed without their daily users were usually rewritten within a year.
Lessons-learned records repeat one finding: tools built away from the people who use them need rebuilding soon after launch.
empath: Engineers are weary of tools that are announced to them. They open up when someone asks about their day first.
People here have seen many launches. They respond to being asked, not told.

d2.title: The First Access Request
d2.scene: The prototype needs live data from the engine test cells. The test operations lead is cautious. An old service account still has broad access to everything, and using it would save weeks.

options.label: Use the old service account that still has broad access
options.aftermath: Data flows by evening. So does a quiet worry about who might notice.

options.label: Co-write a read-only data agreement with the test operations lead
options.aftermath: The lead adds two safeguards of her own, and offers you a standing slot in her weekly review.

options.label: Wait for the standard IT request to run its course
options.aftermath: The request is approved after three weeks. The prototype sits idle, but nothing is exposed.

seer: A security review is scheduled for next month. Anything built on borrowed access will surface in it.
scout: Nobody has audited the old account in two years. A read-only feed could be switched on within a day of agreement.
scholar: The data-handling policy allows read-only sharing for analysis once the data owner has signed off.
empath: The test operations lead has been burned before. She softens when treated as a partner rather than a gate to get around.

d3.title: The Team Question
d3.scene: The prototype works, but it needs one more builder before it can go further. Three people come to mind, and each would change what Bridgeline becomes.

options.label: Recruit the brilliant engineer who prefers to work alone
options.aftermath: The code arrives fast and brilliant. Nobody else can read it.

options.label: Ask the manager to assign whoever is free
options.aftermath: A willing but unconvinced colleague joins. Enthusiasm stays low.

options.label: Invite a sceptical quality engineer to try to break it
options.aftermath: She finds four faults in a day. Then she starts fixing them.

seer: Programmes that survive leadership reviews are the ones that have already answered their sceptics.
scout: The lone engineer’s code is quick but undocumented. The quality engineer’s last review caught three failure cases in a rival tool.
scholar: Review minutes show approvals are blocked more often by missing assurance than by missing features.
empath: The loner cares about the work but not about being coached. The sceptic is quietly curious and has never been asked.

m4.title: Pilot Day
m4.scene: The pilot at one test cell goes well. Two other sites are asking for access, and a conference organiser has noticed your name. Everyone wants Bridgeline now, and each choice sets a different pace.

options.label: Take the pilot on tour at an industry conference
options.aftermath: A conference badge, a stage slot and a stack of business cards. Back at the centre, the backlog grows.

options.label: Open Bridgeline to every site by Friday
options.aftermath: Friday arrives. So do two hundred users and a problem nobody tested.

options.label: Add one more site and fix what the pilot revealed
options.aftermath: The second site finds a slow search and a coarse permissions rule. You fix both before anyone else sees them.

seer: A wide launch before the platform is hardened would draw attention for the wrong reasons. A smaller step compounds quietly.
scout: The pilot exposed slow search beyond one site and permissions that are too coarse. A single extra site would reveal the rest safely.
scholar: Presenting unreleased internal tools outside the company needs legal and export review first, and that takes time.
empath: Every site lead is excited, and that is the danger: each wants to be first. The one who offered to host a trial will give honest feedback.

m5.title: The Data Boundary
m5.scene: Bridgeline now surfaces engine-health insights that customers would love to see. The airline customer’s operations team has asked for direct access, and your account manager is eager to please.

options.label: Give the airline customer a login today
options.aftermath: The airline logs in, and sees more than the contract ever allowed.

options.label: Build a separate customer portal first
options.aftermath: A promising idea and a long road. Word spreads, and a start-up calls.

options.label: Share curated summaries through the existing customer channel
options.aftermath: The airline gets clear, trusted updates and asks for more. Nothing proprietary leaves the building.

seer: Customers want to feel informed. A trusted channel earns more goodwill than raw access ever does.
scout: Design margins sit in the same tables as the health data. Summaries can be generated from the current feed within the week.
scholar: Contract terms and export rules restrict direct access to engineering data. Curated summaries are already an approved route.
empath: The airline wants reassurance, not raw data. A regular briefing from someone they trust would satisfy them.

dr_a.title: The Borrowed Sponsor
dr_a.scene: Your early choices left Bridgeline with a modest reputation. A senior sponsor from procurement offers budget, but she wants the platform reshaped around supplier cost savings. The offer is generous, and it has strings.

options.label: Accept the budget and reshape Bridgeline around cost savings
options.aftermath: The money arrives. The engineers’ priorities quietly leave the roadmap.

options.label: Decline the money and carry on alone
options.aftermath: You keep your independence, and very little else.

options.label: Accept support only with shared goals agreed in writing
options.aftermath: A one-page charter is signed. The sponsor gets her savings metric, and engineering keeps its safety scope.

seer: Sponsors with a single goal pull a product toward it. A written scope keeps the pull in check.
scout: The supplier module is half-built. Reshaping around it would delay the engineering features by months.
scholar: Programmes with a signed charter have outlasted changes of sponsor in this company’s history.
empath: She wants a win, but she respects people who negotiate. What she dislikes most is surprises.

dr_b.title: The Conference Corridor
dr_b.scene: Between sessions at the aerospace conference, a leader from another business unit asks to see Bridgeline. Nearby, a recruiter from a rival firm offers coffee and says he has heard good things.

options.label: Show everything live, including real customer data
options.aftermath: The demo dazzles, until someone reads the customer names on the screen.

options.label: Demonstrate with synthetic data and arrange a follow-up
options.aftermath: The leader leaves impressed, with a meeting booked. Nothing real was shown.

options.label: Skip the demo and accept the recruiter’s coffee invitation
options.aftermath: The coffee is pleasant. The leader from the other unit walks away.

seer: The leader’s unit could become Bridgeline’s biggest user. A strong first impression travels further than the person who made it.
scout: The live demo system is connected to real customer data by default. A synthetic data set is already on the laptop.
scholar: Rules on external disclosure allow synthetic demonstrations without special approval.
empath: The recruiter is friendly, but his interest is in people, not in Bridgeline. The leader is genuinely curious.

dr_c.title: The Start-up’s Offer
dr_c.scene: A young analytics start-up has heard about Bridgeline and offers to run its analytics as a service, quickly and cheaply. The founders are sharp and in a hurry. Your team could use the speed.

options.label: Send them a copy of the data so they can start next week
options.aftermath: They start on Monday. So does a conversation with the security team.

options.label: Turn the offer down and never reply
options.aftermath: The silence is noted, and so is the opportunity you let pass.

options.label: Learn what they do well and bring it in through the supplier process
options.aftermath: The start-up passes the supplier checks slowly, but it does pass. Bridgeline gains a faster engine.

seer: Start-ups with sharp ideas tend to be acquired or to vanish. Whatever you rely on should survive either.
scout: Their prototype is faster than yours on the same sample, but it has never been tested at scale.
scholar: Procurement rules require checks for any outside party that handles company data. They exist for good reason and can be completed in weeks.
empath: The founders want a first big customer more than a quick payout. They will wait if they are treated seriously.

m6.title: The Credit Question
m6.scene: The Leadership Review deck is due tonight. It lists you and your sponsor. The early engineer who built Bridgeline’s search layer is not mentioned anywhere, and she has not asked to be.

options.label: Put your own name on the key slide and send it tonight
options.aftermath: The deck goes out on time. The early engineer reads it on her phone and says nothing.

options.label: Name every builder and invite her to present her part
options.aftermath: She goes quiet, then nods. The slide now carries five names.

options.label: Leave the question of credit until after the review
options.aftermath: Everyone is relieved to avoid an awkward conversation. For now.

seer: People leave quietly after being overlooked. Much of the platform’s best thinking lives in one person’s head.
scout: The search layer has no documentation. Its builder is the only person who can explain it to the reviewers.
scholar: Company recognition guidelines expect every material contributor to be acknowledged in programme reviews.
empath: She has not asked for credit, which is exactly why it matters. She would rather speak for her work than be thanked afterwards.

m7.title: The Incident Alert
m7.scene: Three weeks before the review, a permissions bug lets one site’s maintenance notes appear to users at another site for several minutes. So far, nobody has noticed except you.

options.label: Patch it quietly and tell nobody
options.aftermath: The patch holds. The secret does not.

options.label: Shut Bridgeline down at every site and announce it to the whole company
options.aftermath: The announcement is dramatic, and travels faster than the facts.

options.label: Fix it, report it formally and tell the affected sites plainly
options.aftermath: The report is short and honest. Two site leaders thank you for telling them first.

seer: Hidden problems resurface later and larger. Early honesty buys trust that nothing else can.
scout: The fault was a single permissions rule. It affected notes only, no engine data, and the fix is small.
scholar: The incident procedure requires reporting within a day and provides a short standard template.
empath: The affected sites are not upset about the bug. They would be upset about silence.

m8.title: The Rival Platform
m8.scene: Another team has built Nexus, a platform with a livelier look and a handful of features Bridgeline lacks. Leadership has noticed, and the Review will compare the two. Your people are anxious.

options.label: Quietly withdraw and let Nexus take the stage
options.aftermath: The room is calm. So is the end of Bridgeline.

options.label: Point out Nexus’s weaknesses in front of the Review
options.aftermath: The criticism is accurate and badly timed. The room turns cold.

options.label: Propose combining the best of both with shared ownership
options.aftermath: The rival lead is wary, then relieved. A joint plan takes shape over two long evenings.

seer: Leaders rarely back one of two overlapping tools. They remember whoever made the problem smaller.
scout: Nexus has a better interface but weak search and no assurance record. Bridgeline is the reverse.
scholar: Past programme reviews have rewarded integrated proposals over competing ones.
empath: The Nexus team is as nervous as yours. Their lead has been looking for a way to talk.

m9.title: The Rehearsal
m9.scene: A trusted mentor listens to a full rehearsal of your Review presentation. He is blunt: you have too much good material. You can lead with one of two strong stories, or try to use it all.

options.label: Walk through every feature across sixty slides
options.aftermath: The rehearsal runs forty minutes over. The mentor stops taking notes.

options.label: Open with the hours engineers have won back, in their own words
options.aftermath: A short film of three engineers lands harder than any chart.

options.label: Open with the assurance record and the incident report
options.aftermath: The mentor leans forward when you show the incident report you filed yourselves.

seer: The board remembers one clear story and one clear safety answer. Long lists fade quickly.
scout: The time-saved data is strong, from three sites, with real quotes available. The assurance record is unusually clean for a first release.
scholar: Review guidance suggests a ten-minute opening and an open conversation, not a full tour of the product.
empath: The mentor winces at long decks. The board is split between people-minded and evidence-minded members, and both will be in the room.

m10.title: The Leadership Review
m10.scene: The room is full, the screen is bright, and your presentation lands well. Then the Chair asks the question you hoped to avoid: who owns Bridgeline when the pilot team moves on, and what happens at a site that does not want it?

options.label: Say it is a pilot project and ownership can be decided later
options.aftermath: The Chair writes something down. It is not a note of approval.

options.label: Propose a named cross-site owner and an opt-in rollout with clear measures
options.aftermath: The Chair nods slowly. Somebody at the back starts to smile.

options.label: Offer a handover plan with a small standing team and quarterly assurance checks
options.aftermath: The Chair asks only one follow-up, and it is about the start date.

seer: Leaders approve what they believe will still be cared for in a year. Vagueness reads as risk.
Every approval in the last two years went to a proposal that named an owner. None went to an open question.
scout: A small standing team can be funded from existing budgets. Two sites have already volunteered to be the first opt-in sites.
The numbers work for a small permanent team, and two sites are ready to go first by choice.
scholar: Governance guidance expects a named owner, a handover plan and regular reviews for any shared platform.
Shared platforms here need an owner, a plan for passing it on, and checkpoints. The guidance is explicit.
empath: The Chair is not hostile. She wants to be able to say yes, and is looking for something to hold onto.
She asked the question because she wants to approve. Give her an answer she can defend.

end_alt1.title: The Quiet Shelf
end_alt1.text: Bridgeline never finds its footing. The demos fade, the data goes stale, and the project folder slips down the shared drive. A year later, an engineer stumbles on it and wonders what might have been.
end_alt1.debrief: The early choices decide whether people want a tool at all. Starting from users’ real pain, getting access properly and inviting honest challenge would have built the support Bridgeline needed.

end_alt2.title: The Rollback
end_alt2.text: A rushed expansion exposes information that should never have left its team. Access is frozen within the hour and Bridgeline is switched off for review. The inquiry is fair, thorough and long.
end_alt2.debrief: Pace is a decision, not a virtue. Growing one site at a time and sharing curated summaries instead of raw access would have protected the trust the platform depends on.

end_alt3.title: The Side Project
end_alt3.text: Bridgeline survives, but only as a small tool serving one department. It is useful and tidy, and nothing like the company-wide network you imagined.
end_alt3.debrief: Detours need a clear way back. Help works best when goals and limits are agreed in writing, and outside offers should come in through the proper door.

end_alt4.title: The Burnt Bridge
end_alt4.text: A hasty move costs you something that is hard to rebuild. Key colleagues drift away, and the platform loses the people who understood it best. The Review goes ahead without a strong case.
end_alt4.debrief: Rash choices spend trust faster than it can be earned. Crediting colleagues, owning problems openly and working with rivals would have kept the team whole.

end_alt5.title: The Perfect Pilot
end_alt5.text: Careful to a fault, you keep Bridgeline small, quiet and safe. The Review praises the effort, and funds a rival instead. The pilot carries on, for a while.
end_alt5.debrief: Caution is not the same as care. Staying silent, giving way to a rival and leaving credit unsettled all felt safe, and each of them cost trust or momentum.

end_alt6.title: The Last Question
end_alt6.text: The Review ends politely. Leaders like Bridgeline, but without a focused story or a clear answer on ownership they ask you to come back next quarter. The momentum does not wait.
end_alt6.debrief: The final stretch rewards focus and accountability. A clear opening story and a named owner turn goodwill into a decision.

end_true.title: Bridgeline Goes Live
end_true.text: The Chair smiles. Bridgeline is approved for opt-in rollout across the India sites, with a named owner, a small standing team and quarterly assurance reviews. In the corridor, the early engineer, the sceptical quality lead and the rival team’s lead are already planning the first training session.
end_true.debrief: You started with real users, earned trust through honesty, credited every builder and joined forces with a rival. Ownership and safety, shown openly, made the case.
